title: Al-Ghazali's crisis
hook: the famous scholar leaves his post in doubt and finds the living path (Deliverance from Error)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Junayd of Baghdad, the master of sahw, sobriety, who tied the inner path to the Qur'an and the sunnah. Your line: sober love. Today, a scholar who knew the path by heart, and hadn't walked it.

A professor at the top of his field. Students crowding his lectures, rulers asking his opinion, his books read everywhere. One day he stands up to teach, and can't speak. His tongue won't move. He can't eat. The doctors examine him and say it isn't his body; it's something in his heart. That happened in Baghdad, in the year 1095, to a celebrated scholar. He wrote about it himself, later, in a short book about his search for certainty.
screen: `AT THE TOP OF HIS FIELD.` → `HE STANDS TO TEACH, AND CAN'T.` → `BAGHDAD, 1095.`

segments.voice: His name was Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, a master of law, theology and philosophy, and he taught at the Nizamiyya, the great college of Baghdad. In his book, Deliverance from Error, he says he'd started doubting how anyone can know anything for certain. He went through every school he could find: the theologians, the philosophers, the ones who claimed secret teachers. Finally he turned to the Sufis, read their books, and understood them. Then it hit him. He could explain their path perfectly, and he hadn't walked a single step of it. Knowing the definition of health, he says, isn't being healthy; knowing what makes a person full isn't being full. The Sufi word for the second kind of knowing is dhawq, tasting. As if he could describe honey without ever tasting it. And he saw that his fame, his salary and his reputation were the very things holding him back. That's when his tongue stopped. So he gave away his wealth, except what his family needed, and left Baghdad quietly. For years he traveled, to Damascus, Jerusalem and the holy cities, praying, keeping silent, practicing. In those years he wrote his great work, the Revival of the Religious Sciences, joining the law and the inner path in one book. Later Muslims called him Hujjat al-Islam, the proof of Islam. It started with admitting a doubt. Knowing is not tasting.
screen: `DELIVERANCE FROM ERROR.` · `HE COULD EXPLAIN IT, NOT WALK IT.` · `DHAWQ — TASTING.` · `HE GAVE IT UP AND LEFT.` · then, large: `KNOWING IS NOT TASTING.`

segments.voice: Think of something you're supposed to be sure of, about faith, your work, a relationship or yourself, and notice honestly where you're unsure. Don't solve it and don't panic; al-Ghazali's doubt was the door, not the end, so just name it plainly to yourself. If you pray, bring the doubt to God as it is; if you don't, let it sit beside you without arguing.
Al-Ghazali's crisis. The great scholar who lost his voice, left his post, and went looking to taste what he knew. Today's word.
Your line: knowing is not tasting. Honey has to reach the tongue. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Al-Ghazali's Revival of the Religious Sciences is still read in mosques and study circles, and his account of his crisis is often taught as a model of honest searching within the faith.

chat.says: Why did al-Ghazali leave his teaching post in Baghdad?
options: He could explain the Sufi path but hadn't walked it, so he left to practice.
He stopped believing in God altogether and could no longer teach.
His students stopped coming, so he moved away to find new ones.
chat.meaning: He saw that knowing the Sufis' path isn't walking it: knowing is not tasting. So he gave up his post and went to practice.

notes: Details of the crisis (tongue unable to speak, loss of appetite, physicians' verdict, 1095 at the Nizamiyya) and the analogy of health/satiety are from memory of al-Munqidh; confirm. His own analogy also uses drunkenness.
Travel route (Damascus, Jerusalem, Hebron, Mecca and Medina) and 'years' (about a decade before returning to teach at Nishapur) simplified; confirm.
The Claud Field 1909 English translation is public domain but not on the validator's list, so nothing is quoted.
